div.head: Geþyncðo 1
div.ab: Hit wæs hwilum on Engla lagum, þæt leod 7 lagu for be geþincðum; 7 þa wæron leodwítan weorðscipes wyrðe, ælc be his mæðe, eorl 7 ceorl, þegen 7 þeoden.
Aliquando fuit in Anglorum laga, quod populus et leges consilio regebantur; et tunc erant sapientes populi magni prorsus nominis et pretii, comes et uillanus, tainus et alii singuli pro modo suo.
Hwilum wæs . . . , þæt leod 7 lagu fór be geþingðum; 7 þá wæron þeodwitan wurðscipes wurðe, ælc be his mæðe, ge eorl ge ceorl, ge þegen ge þeoden.
Hit wæs hwilum on Engla lagum þæt leod and lagu for be geþincðum, and þa wæron leodwitan weorðscipes wyrðe, ælc be his mæðe, eorl and ceorl, þegen and þeoden.

Einst galt es in Engländer-Rechten, dass Volk und Berechtigung gemäss Würden ging [sich richtete]; und da genossen die Rathsherren der Nation Ehre, jeder nach seinem Rang, so Adliger wie Gemeiner, so Dienstritter wie Fürst (A. und G., D. und F. H).

Once it was in the laws of the English that people and law went by rank [were ordered]; and then the counsellors of the nation enjoyed honour, each according to his rank, noble as well as commoner, thegn as well as prince (n. and c., t. and p., H).
Once it used to be that people and rights went by dignities, and councillors of the people were then entitled to honour, each according to his rank, whether noble or ceorl, retainer or lord.

In the laws of the English, it once was that people and law were ordered by status, and the people’s councilors were treated with dignity, each according to his rank, noble and commoner, thane and lord.
div.note: D lacks ‘on Engla lagum’ (Liebermann supplies it from the others). ‘þeoden’ is poetic, so the Quadripartitus and Instituta misunderstood it (as in Beowulf 2722, 2869). ‘eorl ⁊ ceorl’ is a rhyming pair, ‘þegen ⁊ þeoden’ alliterating. Another late compiler begins two sentences the same way (Grið 3, 22).
leod and lagu. In alliterative and rhymed formulas words may be used in a vague or archaic sense. “Law” here is used to cover all the complex of rights and obligations of each rank.
ge eorl ge ceorl, ge egen ge eoden. Here eorl retains its old sense of “noble” and egen the element of service rather than of rank.
eorl . . . þeoden: ge eorl ge ceorl, ge þegen ge þeoden D

people and law were ordered by status: The word geþincðu lacks a direct modern English equivalent, and it previously has been translated as “rank,” “status,” “dignity,” and “honor.” thane: A landowner lower in status than a lord, with military obligations to his superior.
